questions.prompt: Under set semantics, what does πcity return for {(1,Hue),(2,Hue),(3,DaNang)}?
options: {Hue,DaNang}
{Hue,Hue,DaNang}
Only {Hue}
questions.explanation: Projection removes duplicates under set semantics. SQL without DISTINCT may behave differently, so the set-semantics assumption matters.

questions.prompt: What does the selection σcity='Hue' do?
options: Keeps only the city column
Keeps tuples whose city is Hue
Renames every city to Hue
Joins all tables that have a city column
questions.explanation: Selection filters rows using a condition; projection chooses columns. These are different operators.

questions.prompt: What does joining R(student,course) and S(course,teacher) on course find?
options: Every pair of tuples, regardless of course
Only courses in R that do not occur in S
Enrollment and teaching pairs with the same course
Tuples paired by row position rather than by course value
questions.explanation: An equijoin requires equal values in the join attributes. A Cartesian product does not impose that condition.

questions.prompt: Why are two separate roles for the City table needed when asking about trips from Hue to Hanoi?
options: Both different city conditions must apply to the same City tuple
Every join must read two physically separate copies
A single role matches both origin and destination without aliases
One role matches the origin and the other matches the destination
questions.explanation: A self-join uses two variables or aliases for two logical roles. It does not require duplicating the stored data.

questions.prompt: R(student,course) is joined with S(course,teacher), and only student is returned. Which expression has the correct logical order?
options: πstudent(R ⋈course S)
σstudent(R × S) without a course condition
πstudent(R) ⋈course S after course has been removed from R
R ⋈course πteacher(S) after course has been removed from S
questions.explanation: The course attribute must remain available to match the join before projecting student. Removing the join attribute first leaves the course condition undefined.

questions.prompt: What is the central message of Codd's theorem in this lecture?
options: Relational algebra and calculus always have the same execution cost
Relational algebra and the appropriate safe relational calculus express the same class of relational queries
Every calculus expression can run without a safe-domain restriction
Declarative queries do not need to be translated into execution plans
questions.explanation: The theorem connects procedural and declarative descriptions of safe, domain-independent relational queries. It does not claim that every arbitrary formula defines a finite query result.

questions.prompt: In {z : ∃x∃y Flight(x,y,z)}, which variable is returned?
options: x and y
All of x,y,z
z
There is no output variable
questions.explanation: z appears in the returned tuple; x and y are existential witnesses. Existential variables do not automatically appear in the output.

questions.prompt: What does {x : City(x,Hue)} express?
options: Every x with City(x,c) where c differs from Hue
Every x, without requiring a corresponding City fact
The cities paired with one fixed x, rather than returning x
The values x for which the fact City(x,Hue) exists
questions.explanation: The fact must exist, and the constant Hue remains fixed. The expression neither negates the condition nor renames the constant.

questions.prompt: Which logical operations primarily form a pure conjunctive query in this section?
options: Existential quantification ∃ and conjunction ∧
Existential quantification ∃ and disjunction ∨ only
Universal quantification ∀ and conjunction ∧, with no existential variables
Negation ¬ and conjunction ∧, without requiring positive atoms
questions.explanation: A positive CQ asserts that witnesses exist that make all its atoms true together. General negation and disjunction go beyond this fragment.

questions.prompt: The query 'students who take DB and have a scholarship' is a CQ. Which query adds an operation outside pure CQs?
options: Students who take DB and AI
Students who take DB but do not have a scholarship
People with at least one enrollment
Person–course pairs that occur together in Enrol
questions.explanation: The absence of a scholarship requires negation. The other positive queries can be expressed using atoms, existential variables, and conjunction.

questions.prompt: In Q(x) :- R(x,y), S(y), which part is the head?
options: R(x,y), S(y)
Only S(y)
Q(x)
The entire database D
questions.explanation: The head specifies the output variables; the body contains the condition atoms. The query's name is distinct from the input relation names.

questions.prompt: In Q(x) :- R(x,y), S(y), what is the role of y?
options: Two independent variables because it occurs twice
A constant named y
A mandatory output variable
An existential variable assigned the same value in both atoms
questions.explanation: A variable name has one consistent assignment throughout a CQ. Because y is absent from the head, its value is not returned.

questions.prompt: Given Enrol(s,c) and Teach(t,c), which CQ finds students taking a course taught by Linh?
options: Q(s) :- Enrol(s,c), Teach(Linh,c)
Q(s) :- Enrol(s,c), Teach(Linh,d)
Q(s) :- Enrol(c,s), Teach(c,Linh)
Q(s) :- Teach(s,c)
questions.explanation: Using the same c joins on the same course. Independent variables c and d would only require Linh to teach some course, not necessarily the student's course.

questions.prompt: What extra condition does Q(x) :- R(x,x) impose compared with Q(x) :- R(x,y)?
options: x and y must always have different values
The two positions in the R fact must have equal values
R must contain at least two tuples
The query creates a new equality relation
questions.explanation: A repeated variable encodes equality between positions. Different variable names do not require different values.

questions.prompt: How does a Boolean CQ differ from a query with output variables?
options: Every table may contain only TRUE/FALSE values
Its body may not contain variables
Its head has no variables; it asks whether a match exists
It always returns YES because it has no output variables
questions.explanation: A Boolean head omits returned variables, but the body still needs a match. Having no output variables does not automatically make the condition true.

questions.prompt: How must a homomorphism treat constants?
options: Change constants like variables if that helps match an atom
Allow different constants to map to the same constant
Remove constant conditions from atoms before matching
Keep every constant unchanged
questions.explanation: The mapping is the identity on constants. Changing a constant would change the meaning of a query condition.

questions.prompt: Let A={R(x,c),S(x)} and B={R(a,c),S(a)}, where c is a constant. Which mapping is a homomorphism?
options: x↦a, c↦c
x↦c, c↦a
x↦a, c↦a
x↦b, c↦c, where b does not occur in B
questions.explanation: The correct mapping sends both atoms into B and preserves c. Matching only one atom or changing c is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Must a homomorphism be injective?
options: Yes; every variable must have a different value
No; two variables may map to the same value
Yes; only constants may have the same image
Yes; if two variables share an image, all atoms lose their meaning
questions.explanation: The definition requires preservation of atoms and constants, not a one-to-one mapping. Distinct variable names alone do not impose a distinctness constraint.

questions.prompt: Let A={R(x,y),S(y)}. The mapping h sends the R atom into B, but S(h(y)) is absent from B. What follows?
options: h is still valid because at least one atom matches
h is valid if the head tuple matches, even though the S atom does not
h is not a homomorphism from A to B
h is valid because the body atoms are joined by OR
questions.explanation: Every source atom must have an image in B. Matching the head or only part of the body is insufficient: a CQ body is an AND conjunction, not an OR disjunction.

questions.prompt: Can R(x,x) map to R(a,b) when a and b are different?
options: Yes, because the relation name R is the same
Yes, if a and b are both constants
Yes, because homomorphisms ignore repeated positions
No; one variable x cannot have two different images
questions.explanation: An assignment is a function, so both occurrences of x must have the same image. The tuple positions must match, not merely the relation name.

questions.prompt: For D={R(a,1),R(a,2),S(1),S(2)}, what does Q(x):-R(x,y),S(y) return under set semantics?
options: {a,a}
The empty set
questions.explanation: There are two matches, but both produce a, so the result set contains one tuple. The number of witnesses is not a bag multiplicity under set semantics.

questions.prompt: For D={R(a,b),R(b,c)}, what does Q(x,z):-R(x,y),R(y,z) return?
options: The empty set, because both atoms use R
questions.explanation: The assignment y=b connects the two facts into a two-step path. Using the same relation more than once is a valid self-join, not an error.

questions.prompt: For D={R(a,b),S(c)} with b different from c, does Q(x):-R(x,y),S(y) return any answers?
options: Yes, a, because an R fact exists
Yes, c, because an S fact exists
No; no value of y matches both atoms
Yes, both a and c
questions.explanation: Conjunction requires the same y in both atoms. Separate facts are insufficient when their join-variable values do not match.

questions.prompt: Why are only the images of head variables used to form Q(D)?
options: Every existential variable must also be returned but is hidden
The head only specifies atom execution order and has no effect on output
Every match always returns both head and body variables
The head defines the result tuple; existential variables only witness a match
questions.explanation: The semantics project each match onto the distinguished output variables. Evaluation neither changes the database nor returns all witness values.

questions.prompt: For D={Link(a,b),Link(b,a)}, what Boolean result does Q():-Link(x,y),Link(y,x) produce?
options: YES, because x=a,y=b is a match
NO, because the same relation name may not be reused
NO, because a Boolean CQ may not share variables
YES, because every satisfiable Boolean CQ is true on every D
questions.explanation: A concrete witness satisfies both atoms here. Being satisfiable on some database does not mean a CQ is true on every database.
